prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by "The Library Plant"?
passage: Maya watered the library plant every Tuesday. One week the leaves drooped, and the soil felt dry and hard. Maya checked the chart on the pot. It said, "Water when the soil is dry." She filled a cup, poured slowly, and waited. By Friday the leaves looked perkier, and the librarian left a note that said, "Thank you for noticing."
choices: The plant looked better because Maya moved it outside.
The note from the librarian made the leaves grow.
Friday sunlight always fixes drooping leaves.
The plant looked better because it finally got water.
explanation: The soil was dry, Maya watered, and then the leaves looked perkier. The story does not say she moved the plant. The answer is "The plant looked better because it finally got water".

prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by "Peaches at the Market"?
passage: Luis held the grocery list while his uncle pushed the cart. At the fruit stand, a sign said three peaches for two dollars. Luis counted six peaches into a bag and checked the list again. His uncle smiled and said they had enough for cobbler. On the way home, the bag bumped Luis’s knee and smelled sweet. He did not eat even one, because the peaches were for sharing.
choices: Six peaches would cost four dollars.
Six peaches would cost six dollars.
The peaches were free with the cart.
Six peaches would cost two dollars.
explanation: Three peaches cost two dollars, so six peaches are two groups. Two dollars plus two dollars is four dollars. The story does not say they were free. The answer is "Six peaches would cost four dollars".

prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by "The Paper Bridge"?
passage: Priya wanted her paper bridge to hold ten pennies. Her first bridge folded in the middle and dropped every coin. She looked at the classroom poster of a real bridge. The poster showed triangles under the road. Priya folded new supports into triangles and tried again. This time the pennies stayed on top, and Priya wrote "triangles" in her notebook.
choices: The triangle supports kept the middle from folding.
The pennies were lighter the second time.
Priya used metal instead of paper.
The poster glued itself to her bridge.
explanation: The first bridge folded in the middle. She added triangle supports and then it held. The story does not say the pennies changed weight. The answer is "The triangle supports kept the middle from folding".

prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by "Rain Plan"?
passage: The class picnic was planned for the grassy field. At lunchtime, clouds piled up and the first drops hit the tables. Coach Ruiz pointed to the gym doors. Students carried blankets, oranges, and the speaker inside. They spread the blankets on the gym floor and started the music. Aisha said the picnic had changed shape, but it was still a picnic.
choices: The students forgot the blankets on purpose.
The gym was already full of rain.
Coach Ruiz wanted the music to stay outside.
Coach Ruiz expected the field to get too wet.
explanation: Drops hit the tables, and Coach Ruiz points to the gym. That action shows the field would not stay a good picnic spot. The answer is "Coach Ruiz expected the field to get too wet".

prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by "Hamster Duty"?
passage: Room 12’s hamster, Nib, needed fresh water every morning. Noah’s name was on Thursday’s chart, but he almost forgot. At the door he turned around and filled the bottle at the sink. Nib stood up and drank right away. Noah checked the food cup too and found it half full. He washed his hands and slid the chart clip to Friday.
choices: The bottle was too heavy for a hamster to use.
Noah moved the chart because the job was canceled.
Nib had already been given water by Friday’s helper.
Nib was thirsty when Noah returned.
explanation: Nib stood up and drank right away after the bottle was filled. That is a clue the hamster wanted water. The answer is "Nib was thirsty when Noah returned".

prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by "The Quiet Birdwatcher"?
passage: On Saturday, Hana and her grandma walked to the pond with a notebook. Grandma whispered that sudden noises send birds away. Hana froze when a heron stepped into the shallow water. She sketched the long beak before the bird lifted off. On the walk home they counted four kinds of birds in the notebook. Hana said the quiet had been a tool, not just a rule.
choices: Grandma asked Hana to clap for every bird.
Sketching made the pond dry up.
The heron might have flown sooner if Hana had shouted.
The heron wanted Hana to chase it.
explanation: Grandma says sudden noises send birds away. Hana stays quiet and gets time to sketch, so a shout would likely have ended the moment sooner. The answer is "The heron might have flown sooner if Hana had shouted".

prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by "New Laces"?
passage: Evan’s new sneakers had long bright laces. On Monday the bows came undone three times before lunch. His friend Lila showed him the bunny-ear steps again. Evan practiced on a chair leg during indoor recess. By Wednesday the bows stayed tied through soccer. He thanked Lila and taught the steps to his little cousin.
choices: Repeating the steps helped Evan’s hands remember them.
Indoor recess made the bows glue themselves.
The laces became shorter on Wednesday.
His cousin tied the shoes for him during soccer.
explanation: He practiced during recess and later the bows stayed tied. The change comes from practice, not from shorter laces. The answer is "Repeating the steps helped Evan’s hands remember them".

prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by "Fort Map"?
passage: Ruby and Andre built a blanket fort between two chairs. They made a map so their little brother could find the reading nook. A blue square stood for the pillow door. A red line showed the tunnel to the flashlight shelf. When the fort sagged, they added a third chair and fixed the map. Their brother followed the colors and crawled in with a book.
choices: The third chair held the blankets up better.
Their brother asked them to remove every chair.
The red line was a real rope.
The map made the blankets heavier.
explanation: The fort sagged, they added a third chair, and then their brother could crawl in. The chair was the fix for the sagging blankets. The answer is "The third chair held the blankets up better".

prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by "A Letter to Cousin Imani"?
passage: Kai wrote a letter instead of sending a short message. He told Imani about the class play and the cardboard castle. He asked what her new school served for lunch. Mom helped him address the envelope and add a stamp. At the mailbox he paused, then let the letter go. Two weeks later a thick reply arrived, full of questions for him.
choices: Imani never opened the letter.
Mom wrote the reply and signed Imani’s name.
Imani was interested and wanted to keep the conversation going.
The reply was empty except for a stamp.
explanation: A thick reply full of questions shows Imani wanted to write back and keep talking. Nothing says the letter was ignored. The answer is "Imani was interested and wanted to keep the conversation going".

prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by "The Patched Kite"?
passage: The wind was finally right, but Tara’s kite had a tear near the corner. Grandpa brought tissue paper, glue, and a scrap of red ribbon. They matched the patch to the tear and let it dry on the porch. While they waited, Tara retied the tail so it would not spin. At the hill the kite climbed, dipped once, and then stayed high. Tara said the patch looked like a small flag of patience.
choices: The tail was removed so the kite would spin more.
The kite flew better because they never patched it.
Waiting for the glue to dry kept the patch from peeling off.
Tissue paper made the kite too heavy to rise.
explanation: They let the patch dry before the hill. Then the kite flew. Drying gave the glue time to hold. The answer is "Waiting for the glue to dry kept the patch from peeling off".

prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by "Almost Snow"?
passage: The forecast had promised snow before recess. Students lined up with hats, but the sky sent cold rain instead. Ms. Ortiz changed the plan and opened the indoor obstacle course. Sofia crawled under the yarn bridge and waited her turn at the hoop. She still checked the window twice, hoping for flakes. At dismissal the rain slowed, and Sofia said, "Maybe the snow is just late."
choices: Ms. Ortiz was surprised that rain is wet.
Sofia was disappointed but still willing to play inside.
Sofia refused to enter the gym.
The hats turned the rain into snow.
explanation: She lined up for snow, then crawled under the yarn bridge and kept looking outside. She played and still hoped, so she was disappointed but willing. The answer is "Sofia was disappointed but still willing to play inside".

prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by "Choir Tryouts"?
passage: Jonah wanted a solo, but his voice cracked on the high note. He asked the music teacher for one extra practice. They broke the line into three smaller pieces. Jonah hummed each piece until the note felt steady. At tryouts he sang the whole line without stopping. He did not get the solo, but he earned a duet with Mei.
choices: Humming made Jonah’s voice lower forever.
A duet means Jonah did not have to sing.
The high note disappeared from the song.
Splitting the line made the high note easier to learn.
explanation: They broke the line into three pieces and he hummed each one until it felt steady. Smaller pieces helped him learn the hard part. The answer is "Splitting the line made the high note easier to learn".

prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by "How Honeybees Help"?
passage: Honeybees visit flowers to drink nectar. Pollen sticks to their fuzzy bodies and rides to the next bloom. That move is called pollination, and it lets many plants make seeds. Apples, almonds, and cucumbers all depend on this kind of help. A hive works as a group, with different bees caring for young, guarding the door, or searching for flowers. People can help bees by planting flowers and avoiding sprays that harm them.
choices: Fewer bees could mean fewer fruits and vegetables.
Cucumbers do not need flowers.
Fewer bees would make apple trees grow faster.
Pollen keeps bees from flying.
explanation: Apples, almonds, and cucumbers depend on pollination. If fewer bees moved pollen, those plants would have a harder time making seeds and fruit. The answer is "Fewer bees could mean fewer fruits and vegetables".

prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by "Garden Soil"?
passage: The school garden has three beds of soil. Clay soil feels sticky and holds water for a long time. Sandy soil feels gritty and lets water drain quickly. The middle bed is loam, a mix that many vegetable roots like. Students add dried leaves to the clay bed so it will not pack so hard. They water the sandy bed a little more often because it dries out.
choices: Clay dries out faster than sand.
A tomato in the sandy bed may need water sooner than one in clay.
Loam is too sticky for any root.
Dried leaves turn sand into rock.
explanation: Sandy soil drains quickly and the class waters it more often. Clay holds water a long time. So a plant in sand can dry sooner than a plant in clay. The answer is "A tomato in the sandy bed may need water sooner than one in clay".

prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by "Triangles in Bridges"?
passage: Look under many bridges and you will see triangles. A triangle keeps its shape when it is pushed at the corners. A square frame can lean and turn into a slanted shape unless it is braced. Engineers add a diagonal bar to make two triangles. That is why cranes, roofs, and bike frames use triangles too. The shape is simple, but it is strong for its weight.
choices: A square frame becomes steadier after a diagonal bar is added.
Bike frames avoid triangles because they are heavy.
A diagonal bar makes a square more likely to lean.
Triangles fall apart when a corner is pushed.
explanation: A square can lean unless it is braced. Adding a diagonal makes two triangles, and triangles keep their shape. So the bar steadies the frame. The answer is "A square frame becomes steadier after a diagonal bar is added".

prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by "Saving Water at Home"?
passage: A dripping faucet can waste more than a gallon of water in a day. Turning the tap off while brushing teeth saves even more. A full dishwasher uses less water than washing the same load by hand with the tap running. Short showers help too, and a timer can make the goal clear. Collected rain is not for drinking, but it can water garden plants. Small habits add up because families use water every single day.
choices: Running the tap while brushing saves the most water.
Garden plants must be watered with drinking water only.
A drip wastes water only during breakfast.
Fixing a drip matters because the waste continues all day.
explanation: The passage says a drip can waste more than a gallon in a day. The leak keeps going, so fixing it stops a whole day of waste. The answer is "Fixing a drip matters because the waste continues all day".

prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by "How a Compass Helps"?
passage: A compass needle is a small magnet. It lines up with Earth’s magnetic field and points toward magnetic north. Hikers still need a map, because north alone does not name the trail. To use both tools, find north on the compass and turn the map until its north matches. Then the paths on the map face the same way as the paths on the ground. A compass can be confused by a nearby magnet or a metal post, so users step away and check again.
choices: Maps work only when the compass is left at home.
A metal post always points to true north.
Earth’s magnetic field turns off near trails.
Standing right next to a metal post could make a hiker read the wrong direction.
explanation: The passage says a metal post can confuse the compass and users should step away. So staying next to the post could give a wrong direction. The answer is "Standing right next to a metal post could make a hiker read the wrong direction".

prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by "Animal Homes"?
passage: Animals build homes that fit their bodies and the weather. A beaver lodge has an underwater door, which keeps many predators out. Termites in hot places build mounds with tunnels that move air. A bird’s nest may be a cup of twigs, or a hole in a cactus, depending on the species. Some animals borrow homes, as hermit crabs do when they move into empty shells. Studying a home can tell you what dangers the animal faces.
choices: Hermit crabs carve new shells from stone.
Termite mounds are built to stop all air from moving.
An underwater door makes it harder for land predators to enter.
An underwater door invites every predator inside.
explanation: The lodge’s underwater door keeps many predators out. A land animal would have trouble using that door, so entry is harder. The answer is "An underwater door makes it harder for land predators to enter".

prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by "From Seed to Tomato"?
passage: A tomato seed holds a tiny plant and a small store of food. When the soil is warm and damp, the seed coat splits. A root grows down, and a shoot grows up toward the light. Leaves open and start making food from sunlight, air, and water. Yellow flowers appear next, and bees may carry pollen from bloom to bloom. After pollination, the flower’s base swells into a green tomato that later turns red.
choices: If the flowers are never pollinated, the plant may not make tomatoes.
The seed’s food store lasts for the whole plant’s life.
A tomato can ripen before the seed sprouts.
Roots grow toward the light instead of down.
explanation: The passage says that after pollination the flower’s base swells into a tomato. Without that step, the fruit stage would not start in the way the passage describes. The answer is "If the flowers are never pollinated, the plant may not make tomatoes".

prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by "Lunchbox Sorting"?
passage: A lunchbox can hold more than food. It can also be a sorting lesson. Apple cores and banana peels belong in compost if your school collects it. A clean plastic bottle can go in recycling, but a bottle with leftover milk should be rinsed first. Foil that is crumpled and full of cheese is too dirty to recycle in many towns. Napkins used for spills usually go in the trash or compost, depending on local rules. The best first step is to learn the signs posted in the school cafeteria.
choices: Compost and recycling are the same bin everywhere.
Banana peels should be rinsed and recycled as plastic.
Leftover milk makes a bottle easier to recycle.
A dirty item may not be recycled even if it is made of plastic or metal.
explanation: The bottle should be rinsed, and dirty foil often cannot be recycled. Dirt can keep a recyclable material out of the bin. The answer is "A dirty item may not be recycled even if it is made of plastic or metal".

prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by "Shadows Through the Day"?
passage: A shadow forms when an object blocks light. In the morning the sun is low, and a student’s shadow can stretch far across the playground. Near noon the sun is higher, so the same shadow grows short. Clouds do not erase shadows completely, but they make the edges softer. You can test this with a stick, chalk, and three marks made at different times. The stick does not change height. The sun’s position does.
choices: The noon mark would be the longest one.
A shadow can form only at night.
Clouds make the stick taller.
The chalk marks would be farther from the stick in the morning than near noon.
explanation: Morning shadows stretch far, and noon shadows are short. Marks at the end of the shadow would be farther away in the morning. The answer is "The chalk marks would be farther from the stick in the morning than near noon".
